extraction.name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
extraction.description: CIFAR-10 is a labeled subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset containing 6000 examples of each of 10 classes (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck). CIFAR-100 contains 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes organized into 20 superclasses. Both datasets were created to enable object recognition experiments on tiny 32x32 colour images.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky
extraction.citeAs: Krizhevsky, A. (2009). Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. Technical Report, University of Toronto.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Paid students labeled a subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset. Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, including hyponyms as defined by WordNet. Labelers were instructed to reject images not belonging to their assigned class based on specific criteria. All submitted labels were personally verified by the authors, and duplicate images were removed.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The tiny images dataset collected by groups at MIT and NYU, assembled by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results per search term. The dataset contains 80 million colour images downscaled to 32x32 across 79000 search terms.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: After collecting images, perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels were removed from the source dataset. For the labeled subsets, duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs. The dataset was divided into training (5000 images per class) and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Paid student labelers were each assigned a class and asked to examine images found with that class (and its WordNet hyponyms) as the search term. Labelers were instructed to reject images not belonging to their class based on criteria: the class name should be a likely answer to 'What is in this picture?', the image should be photo-realistic, it should contain only one prominent instance of the object, and the object may be partially occluded. Labelers were paid a fixed sum per hour. All submitted labels were personally verified by the authors.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The source tiny images dataset has unreliable labels due to the nature of online image search technology, as the search term used to find an image provides only a rough label.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The underlying tiny images dataset has no reliable class labels, making it hard to use directly for object recognition experiments. The noisy labels from search terms are extremely unreliable.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets are intended for object recognition/classification experiments. CIFAR-10 was used for training and testing classifiers. The larger unlabeled tiny images dataset is intended for unsupervised training of deep generative models.

name.evidence: We call this the CIFAR-10 dataset, after the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, which funded the project. In addition to this dataset, we have collected another set – 600 images in each of 100 classes. This we call the CIFAR-100 dataset.

description.evidence: The CIFAR-10 set has 6000 examples of each of 10 classes and the CIFAR-100 set has 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes. Using these labels, we show that object recognition is significantly improved by pre-training a layer of features on a large set of unlabeled tiny images.

inLanguage.evidence: They assembled it by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the lexical database WordNet

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We paid students to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. The labeled subset we collected consists of ten classes of objects with 6000 images in each class... each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all the images which were found with that class as the search term... Furthermore, we personally verified every label submitted by the labelers.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: We paid students to label a subset of the tiny images dataset... each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all the images which were found with that class as the search term... Since each image in the dataset already comes with a noisy label (the search term used to find the image), all we needed the labelers to do was to filter out the mislabeled images.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: The tiny images dataset on which we based all of our experiments was collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU over the span of six months... They assembled it by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the lexical database WordNet. They used several search engines, including Google, Flickr, and Altavista and kept roughly the first 3000 results for each search term... In total, the dataset contains 80 million colour images downscaled to 32x32 and spread out across 79000 search terms.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: After collecting all the images for a particular search term, they removed perfect duplicates and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white... We removed duplicate images from the dataset by comparing images with the L2 norm and using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs and the like. Finally, we divided the dataset into a training and test set, the training set receiving a randomly-selected 5000 images from each class.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: We paid students to label a subset of the tiny images dataset... each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all the images which were found with that class as the search term... The labelers were instructed to reject images which did not belong to their assigned class. The criteria for deciding whether an image belongs to a class were as follows... rai:dataBiases.evidence: The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, although it is extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: A second problematic aspect of the tiny images dataset is that there are no reliable class labels which makes it hard to use for object recognition experiments.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: Using these labels, we show that object recognition is significantly improved by pre-training a layer of features on a large set of unlabeled tiny images... It is, in principle, an excellent dataset for unsupervised training of deep generative models.
